title: 2025-02-11-execpath-stability-persistent-kv-cuda-graphs
next_steps: Jordan: send trimmed benchmark CSV and command lines (by 2025-02-14)
Maya: run the persistent KV cache repro on a 40B quantized build and share logs (by 2025-02-18)
Tom: provision a VPC test subnet and provide SG rules for the on-prem pilot (by 2025-02-17)
Schedule follow-up lab session (60m) to run TRT-LLM vs vLLM on their 2xA100 cluster
action_items: Jordan Lee: Email benchmark artifacts + deck link (due 2025-02-14)
Maya Chen: Attach procfs + CUDA graph traces for persistent-KV-run (due 2025-02-18)

summary: SE-led deep dive profiling kernel routing, CUDA graph instability with persistent KV cache, and tradeoffs between TRT-LLM and vLLM in quantized 3rd-party models. Customer is interested in an on-prem pilot inside VPC with strict egress controls. Key asks: reproducible repro, config surface for kernel selection and fallback, and security artifacts for Private deployment.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Alright thanks everyone for joining. Quick intro, I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and Maya is our performance engineer. We packed a lot into this session — Maya will lead the profiling notes.
[00:16] Maya (SE): Hey all, thanks. I saw the benchmark you sent, Tom — the 40B model with int8 quant and the KV cache enabled. We've been seeing a specific pattern when CUDA graphs are used with persistent KV where latency spikes and graph re-creation churns. I'll try to walk through what we traced.
[00:32] Tom (Nimbus): Yeah, we've been hitting that in our staging cluster. Sometimes requests take 4x longer and the GPU shows recompile kind of behavior.
[00:40] Maya: Right. At a high level there are a few exec paths: the default dynamic kernel path that vLLM uses (not to be reductive), and the TensorRT-LLM optimized graph path where we precompile a graph per sequence-length bucket. When quantization changes memory layout (like 4-bit group sizes) the kernel chooser may flip to a fallback kernel which invalidates existing CUDA graphs.
[01:05] Jin (ML Infra): Can you clarify fallback kernel? I thought TRT had fallback to native kernels when unsupported ops pop up?
[01:10] Maya: Exactly. Fallback means kernel B is used instead of A — often it's less efficient and might not be graphable. The runtime then has two states: stable graph executed, and a recompile path. With persistent KV — meaning we keep KV tensors across requests to avoid recompute — the memory addresses and shapes can change slightly due to allocator fragmentation and cause the graph signature to not match, so the runtime recreates the graph.
[01:38] Evan (SRE): We also see OOM-ish spikes even when GPU memory headroom is fine. Could fragmentation account for that?
[01:44] Maya: Yes, fragmentation + quantized op workspace allocations. We observed in our repro that int8 GEMM workspace can be dynamic and if the quantization promotes a different algorithm (say a cublasLt split kernel), that changes the temp buffers. If CUDA graph snapshot includes those buffers, mismatch causes re-record and latency blip.
[02:05] Sara (Security): From a security standpoint, if graphs are recompiled on the fly, is there any exec path that triggers extra host-side writes or unexpected syscalls? We need to verify audit surface for Private deploy.
[02:15] Priya (Observability): Good point — graph re-records do generate extra host-side work (memory allocation calls, kernel launches) but no new network traffic. We'll provide strace/procfs snippets in the follow-up.
[02:28] Tom: For our pilot we plan to keep all egress blocked; will that affect model fetch or kernel selection?
[02:33] Jordan: No for runtime kernel selection — entirely local. But for initial model provisioning if you use our hosted model catalog, you'd need egress. For Private/on-prem you can seed models via local tarballs or airgap.
[02:45] Jin: Back to TRT vs vLLM — what differences did you see in the latency tail?
[02:50] Maya: vLLM's dynamic scheduler likes to avoid graphing; it focuses on streaming single-token latency with small kernels. TRT-LLM tends to batch and fuse more aggressively, giving better throughput and lower per-token cost when stable, but has higher tail if re-compile happens. In our A/B runs we saw median latency TRT lower by ~18% but P99 worse by 40% under the exact persistent-KV churn scenario.
[03:16] Tom: Hmm, that's consistent. Our SLAs care about P95/P99 more than median.
[03:20] Jordan: That's where policy routing can help — route latency-sensitive requests to dynamic paths or smaller model variants and throughput workloads to TRT-optimized nodes.
[03:29] Jin: How deterministic is the kernel selector? Can we pin kernels per-model?
[03:33] Maya: You can pin kernel profiles in Redwood Dedicated configs — we surfaced kernel selection toggles in the runtime flags. There's also a safe-mode that disables graphing for specific models. We'll share the flag list.
[03:45] Sara: And for KMS — if we do on-prem with our HSM, can Redwood's control plane still orchestrate without egress?
[03:53] Jordan: For Private you can run the control plane locally (no egress) or use our control plane with a secure peering. HSM integration typically needs a reachability path to the KMS endpoint — many customers proxy it internally. We'll provide docs.
[04:05] Maya: I want to call out an oddity: on one run, we saw kernel A used for first 200 tokens, then kernel B after a specific sequence length threshold. The switch wasn't just length but token distribution — more attention heads hitting large kv cache lookups seems to flip heuristics. In TRT this flip triggers graph rebuild.
[04:26] Tom: Is that because sharded KV addresses change order?
[04:29] Maya: Could be. Also allocator patterns in NCCL + UCX pinned memory interplay. We captured a trace where the runtime calls cudaMallocHost in the middle of an inference, which is a red flag for stable graphs.
[04:42] Jin: You mentioned quantization — do 4-bit and 8-bit differ a lot for kernel selection?
[04:46] Maya: Yes. 8-bit stays closer to float kernels sometimes; 4-bit usually requires specialized kernels and packing/unpacking that some graphers don't support, forcing fallback. For some ops we saw a pathway where runtime decides the packed-gemm kernel (very fast) but only if group-size is divisible by 32; unusual group sizes cause fallback. So model conversion parameters matter.
[05:06] Evan: So what's the recommended approach for our pilot? Disable CUDA graphing entirely?
[05:10] Maya: Not necessarily. We recommended three pronged approach: 1) reproduce the issue with our instrumented run (we'll do that), 2) try pinned allocator and deterministic placement to reduce fragmentation, and 3) if instability persists, either pin dynamic kernels for latency-critical endpoints or use TRT-optimized nodes behind routing rules.
[05:28] Jordan: We'll also propose a hybrid config: keep small interactive routes on vLLM nodes (no graphing), bulk inference on TRT nodes with warmup sequences to stabilize graphs.
[05:37] Tom: Are there any quick config knobs we can try today?
[05:39] Maya: Turn on the 'deterministic-alloc' flag, enable the 'graph-warmup' hook that issues warmup requests with a pinned memory pattern, and set quant group-size to 32 during conversion. Those reduced re-records in our lab.
[05:53] Jin: Can you share the exact flags and the warmup script?
[05:56] Maya: Yes — we'll post them. Also note that CUDA graph API can be sensitive to different minor driver versions. We saw one driver patch where the graph handle matching changed heuristics; validate driver versions across nodes.
[06:10] Sara: Any compliance notes about kernel-level telemetry? We need to ensure audit logs don't contain user prompt text.
[06:16] Priya: Our telemetry strips user tokens — we log perf metrics and aggregates, not raw prompts, for Private. We'll send the SOC2/ISO snippets.
[06:24] Tom: You mentioned memory addresses changing causing mismatch. Can we instead canonicalize addresses (mmap tricks)?
[06:28] Maya: Some labs tried that by preallocating a large buffer and sub-allocating deterministically; that reduced churn but complicates multi-tenant memory isolation. For Dedicated or single-tenant Private it's viable. We'll outline tradeoffs.
[06:45] Jordan: Quick interruption — Maya, did you collect nvprof/NSYS traces for their supplied benchmark?
[06:49] Maya: Yes. We ran three configs: baseline vLLM dynamic, TRT-LLM with graphing disabled, TRT-LLM with graphing enabled + persistent KV. The attached CSV has medians and P95/P99 and a gist with NSYS timelines. The big thing in NSYS was repeated cudaLaunchKernel events with identical names but different host timestamps — correlates with graph re-record.
[07:12] Tom: Any anomalous cuBLAS calls?
[07:14] Maya: We observed cublasLt matmul heuristics flipping which is expensive. For quantized matmuls cublasLt may choose a split algorithm that needs additional scratch space; that was the pattern leading to repro.
[07:27] Jin: For the pilot on our 2xA100s, do we need to change NIC configs for UCX?
[07:31] Maya: Ensure CUDA IPC and peer-to-peer are enabled for faster KV shuffles; UCX tuning (tx/rx buffers) matters for large KV fetches. We'll give recommended UCX rc/ud combination.
[07:44] Evan: From an ops point, what telemetry will Redwood provide so we can alert on graph churn?
[07:48] Priya: We emit graph-recompile events, kernel-fallback counts, allocator fragmentation ratio, and GPU busy/idle breakdown by model. Those map to Console dashboards — we'll share JSON for alerts.
[08:02] Tom: Can we have a lightweight probe to detect impending recompile? Some leading indicators?
[08:07] Maya: Yes — snapshot of kernel-selection hash per request and delta of allocator high-water mark. If hash flips repeatedly for same seq-length bucket, alert. We'll provide a small agent script.
[08:20] Jordan: Ok let's move to quantization and model conversion notes quickly.
[08:23] Maya: When converting to 4-bit, use group-size 32 when possible, prefer per-channel scaling for matmuls, and avoid custom fused ops that TRT may not support. Also avoid permutations in attention that create non-contiguous tensors.
[08:39] Jin: Does Redwood support on-the-fly re-quantization as a service?
[08:43] Jordan: We can run conversions as part of onboarding; for Private you can run our conversion tools locally. We don't currently do streaming re-quantization in production — it's an offline step.
[08:53] Tom: For the follow-up lab, can Redwood remote into our cluster or will we run the scripts?
[08:57] Jordan: Either. For security reasons we usually ask customers to run the scripts and share logs; if you prefer we can set up short-lived bastion access scoped to the run. We'll document the necessary access.
[09:09] Maya: One more technical note — graph warmup should mirror production token distributions; if you warmup with zeros or repeated tokens, the internal heuristics may not pick the common kernel. Use representative prompts.
[09:23] Sara: We also need to validate that audit logs for Private deploy are retained within our retention windows and can be forwarded to our SIEM.
[09:30] Priya: Yes, we support S3 sinks for logs and syslog for metrics; retention policies configurable in Private. We'll include a sample retention policy.
[09:40] Jordan: Alright, we'll summarize next steps. Maya will run the repro with instrumented traces, we'll share scripts and flags, Tom will provide model shard layout and cluster details, and we'll schedule the lab.
[09:55] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[10:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts.
[10:04] [END]
